stories.topic: How Ten-Hour Podcasts Changed the Interviewer
stories.summary: Amit started The Seen and the Unseen assuming people have short attention spans, that you must hook them early, and that episodes can't run past 10-15 minutes. All of it proved wrong. The show grew from 15-20 minute single-subject episodes to three-hour deep dives, then to eight-hour-plus oral histories, and recently a ten-and-a-half-hour episode. In his essay 'A Meditation on Form' he worked out that this wasn't the same thing made longer. A five-minute show can be shallow. A long one demands reading all the guest's books, knowing their field and life, and above all listening without interrupting.
stories.insight: A change in length is a change in kind. Long conversations force you to listen to understand rather than to respond, and that changes the person doing the listening.
stories.quote: the key value that I learned from doing those long episodes is that you simply never interrupt.

stories.summary: Bioacoustician Bernie Krause recorded the soundscape of the same spot in California repeatedly between 2004 and 2015, a period that included a drought. To the eye, people couldn't tell how many species had died off or vanished. The sound recording showed it clearly, because each species occupies its own band of frequencies. Amit adds that his editor Gaurav Chintamani says he can do a first cut of an episode just by looking at the waveforms, then listens at double speed.
stories.insight: Sound has a visible structure. Ears and audio charts can pick up changes that eyes miss, whether in an ecosystem or in an edit.
stories.quote: visibly people couldn't really make out the difference of how many species have died or fallen off or whatever. But the soundscape captured everything.

stories.topic: CBGB's: Mess as an Acoustic Feature
stories.summary: If Amit could visit one place at one time, he'd pick CBGB's in New York in 1975, birthplace of American punk and alternative rock, where Television, Patti Smith, the Police and Talking Heads played. Following David Byrne, he explains that the club's crowding, furniture and chatter absorbed sound and killed reverberation. That allowed harmonically complex music and a big return of percussion. His own cluttered home studio, full of bookshelves, works the same way and is easier to record in.
stories.insight: Musical scenes partly grow out of the acoustics of the rooms they were born in. Something that looks like a flaw, such as a messy, crowded room, can be exactly what lets a style work.
stories.quote: And this was a feature, not a bug, because all of it meant that sound was absorbed and there was no reverberation.

stories.summary: In a Rick Beato interview (the show notes link Beato's conversation with Nuno Bettencourt), the guitarist was asked about AC/DC's Angus Young. People mock Young for working with one kind of sound and three or four chords. The guitarist's answer was to consider the circumstances: AC/DC played huge arenas, where you need a wall of sound, and for that his style is perfect. Amit adds that funk never works in a big arena, while metal does.
stories.insight: Judge a style by the conditions it was built for, not by abstract complexity. Different genres are adapted to different settings, and each produces great musicians.
stories.quote: But if you consider the circumstances, right, AC/DC is performing in these large arenas and you want to build that wall of sound. It's absolutely perfect.

stories.topic: Why the Beatles Quit the Stage
stories.summary: Ajay asked why the Beatles stopped touring. Amit's answer came in two parts. First, their months of club gigs in Hamburg around 1962 gave them what Gladwell calls their 10,000 hours and made them a tight unit. Second, after the early hits, audiences got too noisy to play to, and the band wanted to make more evolved music. Ajay added that the best amplification of the time couldn't overcome screaming fans, and that the band was heading towards 'A Day in the Life', which no screaming crowd could take in.
stories.insight: The Beatles' move from live act to studio band was also a change of form. Their later records were made for headphones and home speakers, not stadiums.
stories.quote: a Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band or a Revolver, you know, won't sound good in a live arena. While I Want to Hold Your Hand and Please Please Me will sound great in a live arena.

stories.summary: Jazz uses the instruments it does because early jazz was played in venues without amplification, so loud instruments won. The trumpet rose, and the banjo was preferred to the acoustic guitar until amplification brought the guitar back. Improvisation had a practical origin too. Bands played for paying dancers, and when the written music ran out the dancers still wanted to dance, so the band stretched out with solos.
stories.insight: Features we now treat as the essence of a genre often started as workarounds for practical limits.
stories.quote: So it was almost as coming out of majboori, right? Today if they don't improvise, we'll demand our money back.

stories.summary: When Philips and Sony developed the compact disc, the Sony president was shown a 60-minute disc that could hold more, and he asked for 74 minutes. Amit asked Ajay to guess why, and Ajay got it right: Beethoven's Ninth. The Sony president was a Beethoven fan, and the Ninth Symphony runs 74 minutes.
stories.insight: Standards that feel natural often have arbitrary origins. A whole medium's capacity was set by one executive's favourite symphony.
stories.quote: Yeah, he was a big fan of Ludwig van Beethoven and Beethoven's ninth symphony is seventy four minutes.

stories.topic: Dark Side of the Moon Fit FM Radio
stories.summary: Ajay pointed out how few musicians challenged the LP format, with exceptions like Pink Floyd's 'Echoes', which takes up the whole of side two of Meddle. He had read that in early FM radio, Dark Side of the Moon fit the medium perfectly. Stations could run ads, play the entire album as one block, run more ads, and fill exactly one hour.
stories.insight: Commercial success often comes from fitting the format of the day, and that pressure towards conformity explains why so few artists experiment with form.
stories.quote: you play some ads, play the entire Dark Side of the Moon, and then you play some ads, and that's a one hour block.

stories.topic: Sleepify, 30-Second Beatles and the TikTok Hook
stories.summary: Spotify pays a band once a track has played for 30 seconds, and nothing extra after that. Vulfpeck released Sleepify, an album of 30-second songs, and asked fans to loop it while they slept. The band made a fair bit of money until Spotify caught on. The Pocket Gods released 100BeatlesX30, a large batch of 30-second Beatles covers. TikTok has its own accidental rule: liking a video counts as liking its audio, so the algorithm pushes that sound further. Labels now tell musicians to be as indulgent as they like for the rest of the song, as long as they deliver a viral 15-second hook.
stories.insight: Every new platform creates new constraints and new loopholes. Amit's argument is that these constraints are much looser than the old ones.
stories.quote: Give me that fifteen second hook I can put on TikTok.

stories.topic: The 200,000 Words on Jane Jacobs That Were Cut
stories.summary: Robert Caro delivered The Power Broker to his publisher Robert Gottlieb at one million words. Gottlieb asked his printers what they could do. They said 800,000 words was the most they could bind without the book falling apart. So a 200,000-word section on Jane Jacobs, 'a hero to both you and me' as Amit told Ajay, was dropped. Today it would be put online or published as a separate book. Back then it was simply lost.
stories.insight: The physical limits of a printed book have decided what got published. Every book also has a floor and a ceiling on length, usually 100 to 300 pages.
stories.quote: So there's a full two hundred thousand word section on Jane Jacobs, a hero to both you and me, which was simply cut off.

stories.summary: Drawing on Swapna Liddle's history of Delhi from about 1801 to 1857, Amit describes newspapers that regularly printed poetry. Readers bought papers partly for the shayari, and Emperor Zafar's verses appeared alongside other poets'. Ajay found it unimaginable that an emperor would write poetry at all. One entrepreneur, criticised in his time as too commercial, began publishing newsletters of the poems recited at mushairas, with an essay on the form at the start. Learning poetry stopped being a matter of chance encounters and became fast and systematic. (From a separate Rahul Matthan episode: 19th-century English newspapers were already full of smut and gossip.)
stories.insight: A new medium layered on an old one can speed up learning dramatically. Amit compares the poetry newsletters to what the internet did for his generation.
stories.quote: Newspapers would publish shayari because people would buy newspapers to read them.

stories.topic: Blogging Freed Him from the 800-Word Op-Ed
stories.summary: As a young would-be writer in the 1990s, Amit saw only two options: 800-word op-eds sent to Times of India or Indian Express, or a book of around 200 pages. Blogging in the early 2000s removed those limits. He could write 80 words or 8,000, ignore the news cycle, skip gatekeepers, pick his own style and post whenever he liked. He averaged five posts a day for five years, about 8,000 posts, many just a line and a link, and calls it great writing practice. Social media later split blogging's functions apart, and newsletters revived it by letting writers keep their readers.
stories.insight: When a form stops dictating length, timing and approval, both the amount and the variety of what you write can grow sharply.
stories.quote: I was not bound by form. I could write something in eighty words, I could write something in eight thousand words.

stories.topic: Learning One Format at a Time
stories.summary: Ajay learned writing formats one after another: research papers, then op-eds, then blog posts, then books. Each meant a couple of years fully immersed in that one format. Now he can switch between all of them whenever he wants. Amit pointed out that Ajay had modestly left out his newest form, YouTube.
stories.insight: Each format is a separate skill that takes sustained immersion to learn. Once learned, the skills accumulate and stay available.
stories.quote: There was always a couple of years where I was just deeply inside one format, but all those are now stored in my skull.

stories.summary: Amit recorded an episode of almost ten hours (9 hours 53 minutes) with Rajeshwari Sengupta, 'The Life and Times of the Indian Economy'. YouTube brings in only a small share of his audience, and the 'video' is just a thumbnail over ten hours of two people talking. Even so, it had passed 50,000 views at the time of recording. He also argues that one ten-hour conversation has a different rhythm from ten one-hour episodes.
stories.insight: Audiences will commit to very long content when the form suits it. This is part of why Amit says his longest episodes are his most popular.
stories.quote: Which is bizarre to me, because it's not even a video. It's basically a thumbnail is the only image, and then it's ten hours of two people talking, right? But the content is suited to the form

stories.summary: Miss Excel is an Instagram creator who teaches Excel while dancing to music she loves. Amit says a traditional gatekeeper would have laughed her out of the room, yet she became a star. He vaguely recalls an article saying she earned around $100,000 a week, mainly from courses sold on the side. He notes that he and Ajay have adopted the same approach: build credibility in one place, then sell a separate product.
stories.insight: Without gatekeepers, unusual combinations of skills can find a paying audience.
stories.quote: any gatekeeper would laugh her out of the room

stories.topic: Shah Rukh Khan to One Person at the Airport
stories.summary: Amit is often stopped at airports by someone who thanks him for his work. The people around them have no idea who he is and wonder who this man is. To the person who stopped him, he is a star.
stories.insight: Fame in the creator economy is concentrated in small circles of strong devotion rather than spread across the mainstream.
stories.quote: Nobody around has a faintest clue who I am. They're all looking and going, who's this guy? Right? But for this person, I'm Shah Rukh Khan.

stories.topic: The CRPF Man Who Spotted a YouTuber
stories.summary: Ajay went through airport security with a backpack full of gear, including a tripod. The CRPF officer asked whether he did YouTube, and Ajay said yes. Ajay didn't even have the full Everything is Everything kit with him, but the officer guessed he was a creator anyway.
stories.insight: 'YouTuber' has become a familiar category in everyday Indian life, recognisable even to a security officer.
stories.quote: the CRPF guy said, YouTube karte ho? So I said yes.

recommendations.item: The Art of Podcasting (Episode 49 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: In the intro, Ajay urges listeners to watch it. Amit says it already holds all his podcasting lessons, so he won't repeat them here.
recommendations.reason: Ajay says it's about more than podcasting: it explains how the modern media and creative economies work.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Written when his episodes had reached four and five hours.
recommendations.reason: Where he first worked out that long-form podcasting is a different activity from short-form, not just a longer version. It is the starting point for this episode.

recommendations.creator: Bernie Krause (interviewed by Erin Robinsong)
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes for Krause's frequency chart and the California soundscape recordings Amit showed.
recommendations.reason: The source for how habitat shapes birdsong and how a soundscape revealed species loss during a drought.

recommendations.creator: David Byrne
recommendations.context: The main source for the music chapter, and repeated in the closing recommendations.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a masterpiece and gives it to everyone he meets. It shows how venues and technology, from cathedrals to CBGB's, shaped the music played in them.

recommendations.item: Nuno Bettencourt interviewed by Rick Beato
recommendations.creator: Rick Beato
recommendations.context: The Rick Beato interview the show notes link for the defence of Angus Young.
recommendations.reason: Makes the case that AC/DC's simple wall of sound is ideal for arenas, a reminder to judge music against its circumstances.

recommendations.item: How Bing Crosby Made Silicon Valley Possible
recommendations.creator: Ted Gioia
recommendations.context: Cited while explaining how the microphone created crooning.
recommendations.reason: Shows how a new technology produced a new style of singing: soft, close-up and intimate, as with Bing Crosby and Frank Sinatra.

recommendations.creator: Vulfpeck
recommendations.context: Example of a band exploiting Spotify's 30-second payout rule.
recommendations.reason: An album of 30-second tracks meant to loop all night while fans slept, and it made the band money until Spotify caught on.

recommendations.creator: The Pocket Gods
recommendations.context: Shown on screen right after Sleepify.
recommendations.reason: A large batch of 30-second Beatles covers, another response to the same streaming rule.

recommendations.item: The Seven Basic Plots (Episode 69 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recalled while discussing three-minute songs and forty-minute albums.
recommendations.reason: Makes the point that a constraint doesn't stop great work. The Beatles and the Stones did brilliant things inside fixed formats.

recommendations.creator: Ulrich Boner
recommendations.context: Shown on screen as an example of what an early printed book looked like.
recommendations.reason: A visual starting point for the story of how printing and distribution shaped writing.

recommendations.creator: Robert Caro
recommendations.context: Amit calls it one of his favourite books, then tells the story of its million-word manuscript.
recommendations.reason: A masterful biography of Robert Moses, a portrait of New York City, and a study of how power corrupts. It also shows how the limits of print cut out a 200,000-word section on Jane Jacobs.

recommendations.item: Rahul Matthan Seeks the Protocol (Episode 360 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: One of two episodes he cites that describe 19th-century newspapers.
recommendations.reason: Shows that 19th-century English newspapers were already full of smut and gossip, so this is nothing new.

recommendations.item: Swapna Liddle and the Many Shades of Delhi (Episode 367 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: He calls it a lovely episode and one of his favourites.
recommendations.reason: The conversation behind the stories of poetry in Delhi's newspapers and the mushaira newsletters.

recommendations.creator: Swapna Liddle
recommendations.context: Liddle's history of Delhi from about 1801 to 1857.
recommendations.reason: One of Amit's favourite history books. It covers a period of transition when newspapers, newsletters and printed poetry took off.

recommendations.context: Amit's favourite TV show, discussed in the audiovisual chapter.
recommendations.reason: It ignores the habits of traditional cinema: no hook, no background music other than what plays within scenes, fifteen or sixteen major characters, and a story that unfolds slowly over seasons. It shows that TV can now do what a novel does.

recommendations.item: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (Episode 402 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The marathon episode with Ajay, who jokes that he's still waiting for his gold medal for the ten-and-a-half-hour recording.
recommendations.reason: An example of the extreme long-form conversations Amit says are now possible.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of the Indian Economy (Episode 387 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: An episode of almost ten hours with Rajeshwari Sengupta.
recommendations.reason: Although the YouTube version is just a thumbnail and ten hours of talk, it has passed 50,000 views, which Amit takes as evidence that the content suits the form.

recommendations.item: If You Are a Creator, This Is Your Time
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: He asks listeners to read this newsletter post when Ajay asks how creators find audiences.
recommendations.reason: It sets out his five reasons this is a good time for creators: means of production, no gatekeepers, no constraint of form, direct reach to audiences, and direct monetisation.

recommendations.creator: Kevin Kelly
recommendations.context: Introduced as 'an important concept' for listeners.
recommendations.reason: Argues that creators don't need to scale: a thousand fans paying $100 a year is a living. It sounded unrealistic when written, and Amit says it is now happening.

recommendations.creator: Li Jin
recommendations.context: Linked alongside Kelly's essay.
recommendations.reason: A hundred fans paying $1,000 a year gives the same income from a smaller, more committed audience.

recommendations.creator: Bari Weiss
recommendations.context: Weiss left the New York Times and started a Substack publication that Amit recently read is valued at $100 million.
recommendations.reason: Evidence that one person starting a newsletter can build a very large business without a mass-media gatekeeper.

recommendations.item: Shephali Bhatt Is Searching for the Incredible (Episode 391 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with journalist Shephali Bhatt, mentioned in reply to Ajay's survivor-bias question.
recommendations.reason: Bhatt wrote a piece reporting that more than one lakh Indian creators (about 1,12,000) earn between one and ten lakh rupees a month, which counters the survivor-bias worry.

recommendations.creator: Ted Gioia
recommendations.context: Closing recommendations.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls Gioia a deep meta-thinker about music and the music business.

recommendations.creator: Rick Beato
recommendations.context: Closing recommendations.
recommendations.reason: A great music channel that Amit enjoys a lot and loves, though he says it isn't much about thinking on form.

recommendations.creator: Don Norman
recommendations.context: His main closing recommendation.
recommendations.reason: A masterpiece. It shows that everything around us looks and works the way it does for particular reasons we have stopped noticing.

recommendations.creator: Led Zeppelin
recommendations.context: Ajay's closing pick.
recommendations.reason: Since the episode talked so much about music, he chose a song of the day.

core_ideas.concept: Form Shapes Content, Content Shapes Character
core_ideas.explanation: The format you work in decides what content is possible, and producing that content changes you. A five-minute show can only be rapid-fire, while a ten-hour one requires deep preparation and listening without ego, which makes you a different kind of person. Some content also suits only one form, so pick the form to fit what you want to say.
core_ideas.quote: You know, I say form shapes content, and content shapes character.

core_ideas.explanation: Different birds sound different because of their environments. In dense rainforest, repeated calls in a narrow frequency band get through. Birds near the forest floor call at lower pitches that are absorbed less. Water birds have calls that carry across water, and long-distance callers use buzzing sounds that cut through. What seems instinctive is the product of natural selection by surroundings.
core_ideas.quote: But actually everything is contingent and everything comes out of form.

core_ideas.concept: Music Takes the Shape of Its Venue
core_ideas.explanation: Outdoor music tends to be percussive because rhythm carries over distance, as in tribal drumming or Ganpati processions. Gothic cathedrals echo for more than four seconds, so their music became modal, slow and harmonically simple. Bach often played a pipe organ in smaller churches, larger halls produced Mahler, low-echo clubs supported complex rock, and arenas favour metal.
core_ideas.quote: So if you're sitting out in the open as we are now, the optimal kind of music is percussive music.

core_ideas.concept: There Is No Hierarchy of Forms
core_ideas.explanation: Western classical music is not 'more evolved' than drumming, and a book is not the highest form of writing. Each genre and format is an adaptation to its circumstances, and each has its great practitioners. So follow what moves you, without judgment or hesitation.
core_ideas.quote: But actually there's no hierarchy, there's no value judgment. Particular kinds of music sound the way they do because of circumstances.

core_ideas.explanation: The three-minute pop song came from the 78 RPM record's capacity, and it also suited radio. The 40-minute album came from Columbia's 1948 LP, about 20 minutes per side, and the CD's 74 minutes came from Beethoven's Ninth. Listeners then came to expect these formats, so the conventions outlasted the limits that created them. Nostalgia for the concept album is really nostalgia for a storage constraint.
core_ideas.quote: dude, the concept album came about because there was a constraint in the storage

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay observes that few artists experimented with form even when they could, because of strong pressure to conform. Amit adds a selection effect: an eight-minute song doesn't get radio play unless you're already Pink Floyd, so formats get flattened. He also notes that great work is still possible inside a constraint.
core_ideas.quote: I guess there are powerful conformist forces that want you to fit into a mainstream world.

core_ideas.explanation: Adam Smith could not have had his ideas before books existed. Long-form writing lets a thinker build layers of thought on earlier layers, so it is part of how the thinking happens, not just a record of it.
core_ideas.quote: The fact that he can have the thoughts he did is that by writing, he is actually making himself a better thinker.

core_ideas.concept: A Film Is a Short Story, a Streaming Series Is a Novel
core_ideas.explanation: A 90-minute feature has one main narrative arc and one central tension, like a short story. Streaming platforms made novel-like screen storytelling possible, with many characters and storylines unfolding over seasons. People binge eight hours at a stretch, which undercuts the short-attention-span argument.
core_ideas.quote: Actually a feature film of ninety minutes is equal to a short story. It's not a novel.

core_ideas.explanation: In cinema the camera is about as far from the actor as the screen is from the viewer, which suits westerns and car chases. Television is a couple of metres away, which suits sitcoms. YouTube is in your hand, with close-up faces. Microphones made crooning possible, while stage actors without amplification had to project. Radio is shaped by commercial pressure to be like five people in a car, broad and mainstream. A podcast feels intimate enough to go deep and niche.
core_ideas.quote: Whereas a podcast is a voice in your head.

core_ideas.concept: Five Ways the World Changed for Creators
core_ideas.explanation: Creators now have the means of production, no gatekeepers in the way, no constraint of form, direct reach to audiences and direct monetisation. The old model, where a newspaper gathered readers' attention, sold it to advertisers and paid the writer a small share, was clumsy and existed because micropayments involved too much friction. Your attention is not free either, since time is money.
core_ideas.quote: Point number four is we can reach audiences directly. And point number five is we can monetize from audiences directly.

core_ideas.explanation: In the past only the very top artists earned anything, while a mediocre engineer or lawyer lived comfortably. That pressure to reach a mass audience shaped what artists made. Kevin Kelly's 1,000 fans paying $100 a year, or Li Jin's 100 fans paying $1,000, frees creators from needing scale.
core_ideas.quote: Kelly's point is you don't need to scale anymore.

core_ideas.concept: Better to Be Loved by a Few Than Liked by Many
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's adopted motto from Paul Graham, originally said about startups. People who love your work will pay, support you and stay with you. People who merely like it engage shallowly and like plenty of other things too.
core_ideas.quote: it is better to be loved by a few than liked by many.

core_ideas.concept: The Creator Economy Is Not Survivor Bias
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay asked whether this is like rock bands, where a handful break through and most earn nothing. Amit says no: over a lakh Indian creators earn between one and ten lakh rupees a month, and many would never have reached the mainstream. More people alive, more leisure, cheap tools and a far wider range of influences mean there should be more active creators today than in all earlier history combined. Many are known only within their niches.
core_ideas.quote: We should have a Shakespeare in every nukkad.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit learns a subject by jumping in, experimenting, and only later working out the first principles. His apparent expertise is assembled afterwards from a lot of trial and error.
core_ideas.quote: Just do stuff and you'll learn from it.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay opens by calling Amit 'more than just an atom in a kinetic theory of gases' since he also contemplates the theory. Amit: 'If I was sexy, I would be an atom bomb.' When Ajay pushes the metaphor, Amit says the answer to why atoms bounce around is 'we have no idea. Life is probably meaningless, we're all gonna die.'
On the ten-and-a-half-hour episode. Ajay: 'I'm still waiting for my gold medal.' Amit: 'until the podcast comes to an end, you can't get the gold medal. You are the provisional gold at the moment.'
Pointing out the birdsong in the background: 'The twittering of birds, not twitter... or perhaps we should call the Xing of birds.'
On rainforest birds that repeat the same narrow-frequency call so something gets through: 'Like so many columnists, in fact.'
On why open-air processions are percussive: 'You will not hear khayals and thumris while people are marching to the beach.'
Amit's off-colour aside about the author of Der Edelstein: 'Apparently his wife used to say that every morning I wake up and I find that Boner has a boner. But leaving that aside...'
On early crooners singing softly into the mic: 'much as some podcasters can do with their dynamic microphones.'
Amit calls the mushaira newsletters exposure to 'a large LLM, as it were', using AI vocabulary for a 19th-century reader's sample size.
On binge-watching: 'For those of us who have office, we miss office the next day. I don't have to.'
Amit says the mediocre artist is 'starving in an attic as the cliche goes.' Ajay: 'therefore it's called having a girlfriend with a job.'

Ajay: 'owing to the shortage of followers, the production of leaders has been discontinued.' Amit objects that not everyone is a creator, and Ajay does the maths: about 10^8 potential followers and 10^5 creators, 'so there's still like an average of thousand each.'
Winston Churchill, quoted by Ajay: 'we make our buildings and then our buildings make us.'
Stephen Covey: 'we listen to respond, we don't listen to understand.' Amit uses it to describe the listening long conversations require.
Stewart Brand, quoted by Ajay: 'We are as gods and we might as well learn to live like that.'
Malcolm Gladwell's 10,000 hours, applied to the Beatles' Hamburg years around 1962.
'It ain't over till the fat lady sings', used to explain why opera singers had to project before the microphone.
Sturgeon's Law, 'ninety five percent of everything is crap', which Amit cites while arguing that great art is still being made in Instagram reels and TikTok.
The Doordarshan-era half-hour TV show: 24 minutes of content plus two 3-minute ad breaks.
Timothy Snyder's On Tyranny, about 12,000 words, as the rare short book a great writer can get away with.
Amit calls Bari Weiss 'a fellow winner of the Bastiat Prize.'
The Peter Cat Recording Company, loved by Amit and crew Nomsita and Vaishnav: 'never gonna be the Beatles in terms of scale', but the Beatles to their devoted fans.
The era of building temples to Amitabh Bachchan, which Amit thinks we may have seen the last of as fame moves into niches.
